title: Integrated Math 1
blurb: Unit-by-unit practice for Integrated Math 1 — quantities and expressions through transformations, coordinate geometry and data, every unit with its own problem collection.

units.title: Quantities & the Structure of Expressions
units.blurb: Units and precision, reading an expression's structure, creating equations from a situation, and rearranging formulas.

units.title: Linear Equations & Inequalities
units.blurb: Justified solving step by step, fractions and the special cases, the inequality flip rule, compound and absolute value.

units.title: Functions & Sequences
units.blurb: The one-output rule, function notation with domain and range, and arithmetic and geometric sequences.

units.title: Linear Functions & Modelling
units.blurb: Slope as a rate, slope-intercept and point-slope forms, parallel and perpendicular lines, and reading a linear model.

units.title: Systems of Equations & Inequalities
units.blurb: Graphing, substitution and elimination, classifying by slope, and shaded feasible regions.

units.title: Exponential Functions & Growth
units.blurb: Growth and decay factors, graphing, linear against exponential, and building a model from data.

units.title: Transformations & Congruence
units.blurb: Translations, reflections and rotations, sequences and symmetry, and congruence defined by rigid motion.

units.title: Connecting Algebra & Geometry
units.blurb: Distance and midpoint, parallel and perpendicular by slope, partitioning a segment, and coordinate proof.

units.title: Describing Data
units.blurb: Centre and spread, comparing distributions, two-way frequency tables, and lines of fit against causation.

forms.title: Evaluating expressions

forms.title: Two-step linear equations
forms.skill: Undo addition, then undo multiplication — in that order.

variants.statement: Solve: $2x - 2 = 2$.
variants.explanation: Undo the addition first: $2x = 4$, then divide by $2$: $x = 2$. Check: $2\cdot 2 - 2 = 2$.

forms.title: Rational equations
forms.skill: Clear the denominator, solve, then verify the denominator isn't zero.

variants.statement: Solve: $\dfrac{x + 4}{x + 2} = 2$.
variants.explanation: Multiply both sides by $x + 2$ (allowed since $x \ne -2$): $x + 4 = 2(x + 2)$, which gives $x = 0$. The denominator is nonzero there, so it is valid.

forms.title: Units, rates and precision
forms.skill: Convert by multiplying by 1 in disguise; the units tell you which way to divide.

variants.statement: A bus travels at $45$ km/h. Express this speed in m/min.
variants.explanation: $1$ km $= 1000$ m and $1$ h $= 60$ min, so multiply by $\frac{1000}{60}$: $45 \times \frac{1000}{60} = 750$ m/min. Dividing by $3600$ instead would give m/s, and multiplying by $1000$ alone converts the distance but leaves the time in hours.

variants.statement: A block of mass $240$ g occupies $3$ cm$^3$. What is its density in g/cm$^3$?
variants.explanation: Density is mass per unit volume: $\frac{240}{3} = 80$ g/cm$^3$. Dividing volume by mass gives cm$^3$/g — the reciprocal unit, which is the usual slip.

forms.title: Reading the structure of an expression
forms.skill: Terms are separated by + and -; factors are multiplied. Naming the part is the skill.

variants.statement: In the expression $3(x + 5) - 2$, which is a FACTOR of the first term?
variants.explanation: The first term is the product $3 \cdot (x + 5)$, so its factors are $3$ and $(x + 5)$. $x$ alone is a term inside the bracket, not a factor of the whole product, and $2$ is a separate term.

variants.statement: In the expression $4(x + 7) - 3$, which is a FACTOR of the first term?

variants.statement: Rewritten to reveal its structure, $4x^2 - 9$ is a difference of two squares only when which condition holds?
variants.explanation: $4x^2 - 9 = (2x)^2 - 3^2 = (2x - 3)(2x + 3)$. The pattern needs each part to BE a square; the sign of $x$ and the relative size of the coefficients are irrelevant.

forms.title: Creating an equation from a situation
forms.skill: A one-off charge is a constant; a per-unit charge is a coefficient.

variants.statement: A gym charges a one-time joining fee of $5\,000$₮ plus $800$₮ per visit. Which equation gives the number of visits $v$ that make the total $21\,000$₮?
variants.explanation: The fee is paid once, so it is a constant; the per-visit charge scales with $v$. That is $5\,000 + 800v = 21\,000$. Folding the fee into the rate would charge it every visit.

variants.statement: A rectangle's length is $7$ cm more than $4$ times its width $w$. Which expression gives the PERIMETER?

variants.statement: Two numbers add to $12$ and one is $5$ more than the other. If the smaller is $n$, which equation models this?

forms.title: Rearranging a formula
forms.skill: Undo operations outward-in, and never divide a sum before you have split it.

variants.statement: Rearrange $A = \frac{1}{2}bh$ to make $h$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Multiply both sides by $2$ then divide by $b$: $2A = bh$, so $h = \frac{2A}{b}$. Dividing by $2$ instead of multiplying is the common slip.

variants.statement: Rearrange $P = 2l + 2w$ to make $w$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Subtract $2l$ first, then halve: $P - 2l = 2w$, so $w = \frac{P-2l}{2}$. (This equals $\frac{P}{2} - l$ — but only if you distribute the halving over BOTH terms, which the shown alternative does not.)

variants.statement: Rearrange $V = \pi r^2 h$ to make $h$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Divide by everything multiplying $h$: $h = \frac{V}{\pi r^2}$. Dropping the square treats the radius as linear.

variants.statement: Rearrange $C = \frac{5}{9}(F - 32)$ to make $F$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Multiply by $\frac{9}{5}$ then undo the subtraction: $\frac{9}{5}C = F - 32$, so $F = \frac{9}{5}C + 32$. The $+32$ must land OUTSIDE the scaling.

variants.statement: Rearrange $y = mx + b$ to make $m$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Subtract $b$ before dividing: $y - b = mx$, so $m = \frac{y-b}{x}$. Dividing first would have to divide $b$ by $x$ as well.

variants.statement: Rearrange $S = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ to make $S$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Expanding the numerator: $n(n+1) = n^2 + n$, so $S = \frac{n^2+n}{2}$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $A = P(1 + rt)$ to make $r$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Divide by $P$, subtract $1$, divide by $t$: $\frac{A}{P} - 1 = rt$, and $\frac{A-P}{P} = rt$, so $r = \frac{A-P}{Pt}$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $d = \frac{m}{V}$ to make $V$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Multiply by $V$ then divide by $d$: $dV = m$, so $V = \frac{m}{d}$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $E = mc^2$ to make $m$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Divide by $c^2$: $m = \frac{E}{c^2}$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $F = \frac{9}{5}C + 32$ to make $C$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Undo the $+32$ first, then the scaling: $F - 32 = \frac{9}{5}C$, so $C = \frac{5}{9}(F-32)$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $v = u + at$ to make $t$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Subtract $u$ then divide by $a$: $t = \frac{v-u}{a}$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $A = \frac{(a + b)h}{2}$ to make $b$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Multiply by $2$, divide by $h$, subtract $a$: $\frac{2A}{h} = a + b$, so $b = \frac{2A}{h} - a$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $A = \frac{1}{2}bh$ to make $b$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Symmetric to solving for $h$: $2A = bh$, so $b = \frac{2A}{h}$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $P = 2l + 2w$ to make $l$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Subtract $2w$, then halve: $l = \frac{P-2w}{2}$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $V = \pi r^2 h$ to make $r^2$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Divide by $\pi h$: $r^2 = \frac{V}{\pi h}$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $v = u + at$ to make $a$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Subtract $u$, divide by $t$: $a = \frac{v-u}{t}$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $A = P(1 + rt)$ to make $P$ the subject.
variants.explanation: $P$ multiplies the bracket, so divide by it: $P = \frac{A}{1+rt}$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $S = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ to make $n(n+1)$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Multiply both sides by $2$: $n(n+1) = 2S$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $d = \frac{m}{V}$ to make $m$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Multiply both sides by $V$: $m = dV$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $C = \frac{5}{9}(F - 32)$ to make $F - 32$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Multiply by the reciprocal $\frac{9}{5}$: $F - 32 = \frac{9}{5}C$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $y = mx + b$ to make $b$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Subtract $mx$ from both sides: $b = y - mx$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $A = \frac{(a + b)h}{2}$ to make $h$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Multiply by $2$, divide by $(a+b)$: $h = \frac{2A}{a+b}$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $E = mc^2$ to make $c^2$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Divide by $m$: $c^2 = \frac{E}{m}$.

variants.statement: Rearrange $P = 2l + 2w$ to make $l + w$ the subject.
variants.explanation: Factor the $2$ out: $P = 2(l + w)$, so $l + w = \frac{P}{2}$.

variants.statement: Find the slope of the line through $(1,\ 2)$ and $(5,\ 10)$.
variants.explanation: Slope is rise over run: $\frac{10 - (2)}{5 - (1)} = 2$. Both differences must be taken in the SAME order — reversing one of them flips the sign, and inverting the fraction answers 'run over rise'.

forms.title: Parallel and perpendicular slopes
forms.skill: Parallel keeps the slope; perpendicular flips it AND negates it.

variants.statement: A line has slope $\frac{2}{3}$. What is the slope of any line PERPENDICULAR to it?
variants.explanation: Perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals: flip $\frac{2}{3}$ to $\frac{3}{2}$ and negate, giving $-\frac{3}{2}$. Their product is $-1$. Negating without flipping (or flipping without negating) leaves a line that is not perpendicular.

variants.statement: A line has slope $\frac{2}{3}$. What is the slope of any line PARALLEL to it?
variants.explanation: Parallel lines have EQUAL slopes, so the slope is again $\frac{2}{3}$. The negative reciprocal $-\frac{3}{2}$ would be perpendicular instead.

forms.title: Reading a linear model in context
forms.skill: The coefficient is a rate per unit; the constant is the one-off.

variants.statement: The cost of a phone plan is $C = 15\,000 + 2\,500n$ ₮, where $n$ is the number of months. What does the $2\,500$ represent?
variants.explanation: The coefficient of $n$ is the RATE — how much the cost rises per extra month. The constant $15\,000$ is the sign-up fee, paid once regardless of $n$.

variants.statement: The cost of a phone plan is $C = 15\,000 + 2\,500n$ ₮, where $n$ is the number of months. What does the $15\,000$ represent?
variants.explanation: The constant term is the value when $n = 0$ — the sign-up fee, owed before any month at all. The coefficient $2\,500$ is the per-unit rate.

variants.statement: The cost of a phone plan is $C = 15\,000 + 2\,500n$ ₮. Find the cost for $4$ months.
variants.explanation: Substitute $n = 4$: $C = 15\,000 + 2\,500 \times 4 = 25\,000$₮. Forgetting the constant charges only the variable part.

forms.title: One solution, none, or infinitely many
forms.skill: Compare slopes first: different = one, same+different intercept = none, identical = infinite.

variants.statement: How many solutions does the system $y = 2x + 3$ and $y = 2x + 7$ have?
variants.explanation: Both lines have slope $2$ but different intercepts ($3$ and $7$), so they are parallel and never meet — no solution.

variants.statement: How many solutions does the system $y = -3x + 1$ and $y = -3x + 5$ have?
variants.explanation: Both lines have slope $-3$ but different intercepts ($1$ and $5$), so they are parallel and never meet — no solution.

variants.statement: How many solutions does the system $y = 4x - 2$ and $y = 4x + 6$ have?
variants.explanation: Both lines have slope $4$ but different intercepts ($-2$ and $6$), so they are parallel and never meet — no solution.

variants.statement: How many solutions does the system $y = 5x$ and $y = 5x - 4$ have?

forms.title: Growth and decay factors
forms.skill: Factor = 1 + rate for growth, 1 - rate for decay. The rate alone is not the factor.

variants.statement: A quantity grows by $5\%$ each year. What is its growth FACTOR?
variants.explanation: Growing by $5\%$ means keeping $100\%$ and adding $5\%$, so multiply by $1 + \frac{5}{100} = \frac{21}{20}$. The rate $\frac{1}{20}$ alone is what you ADD, not what you multiply by.

forms.title: Evaluating an exponential model
forms.skill: Only the base takes the exponent; compounding is repeated multiplication.

variants.statement: For $f(t) = 5 \cdot 2^t$, find $f(3)$.
variants.explanation: Only the base is raised to the power: $2^{3} = 8$, then multiply by $5$ to get $40$. Raising the whole product $5 \cdot 2$ to the power is the usual error.

variants.statement: For $f(t) = 3 \cdot 2^t$, find $f(4)$.
variants.explanation: Only the base is raised to the power: $2^{4} = 16$, then multiply by $3$ to get $48$. Raising the whole product $3 \cdot 2$ to the power is the usual error.

forms.title: Linear against exponential
forms.skill: Constant differences = linear; constant ratios = exponential. Exponential always wins eventually.

variants.statement: Model A adds $10$ each step; Model B multiplies by $2$ each step. Over enough steps, which grows faster?
options: Model B — exponential eventually beats any linear
they grow at the same rate
variants.explanation: Adding a constant gives LINEAR growth; multiplying by a constant $>1$ gives EXPONENTIAL growth. Exponential growth always overtakes linear growth eventually, however large the linear step or however small the head start.

forms.title: Half-life and repeated halving
forms.skill: Count how many half-lives fit, then halve that many times — decay never reaches zero.

variants.statement: A sample of $80$ g has a half-life of $5$ years. How much remains after $10$ years?
variants.explanation: $10$ years is $2$ half-lives, so halve $2$ times: $80 \div 2^{2} = 20$ g. Subtracting half the ORIGINAL each time would reach zero, which decay never does.

forms.title: Image under a reflection or rotation
forms.skill: Apply the coordinate rule; every wrong option is a different rigid motion.

variants.statement: The point $A(3,\ 1)$ undergoes a reflection in the $x$-axis. What are the coordinates of its image?
variants.explanation: This transformation keeps $x$ and negates $y$, so $(3,\ 1) \mapsto (3,\ -1)$. Each wrong option is the image under a DIFFERENT rigid motion — the rule has to be applied, not guessed from the picture.

forms.title: Choosing the congruence criterion
forms.skill: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, HL — and AAA, which proves similarity, not congruence.

variants.statement: In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$, $AB = DE = 7$, $BC = EF = 9$ and $AC = DF = 12$. Which criterion proves them congruent?
variants.explanation: Three pairs of equal SIDES fix the triangle completely. AAA is never a congruence criterion — equal angles give SIMILAR triangles, which may differ in size.

variants.statement: In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$, $AB = DE = 7$, $\angle B = \angle E = 50°$ and $BC = EF = 9$. Which criterion proves them congruent?
variants.explanation: The equal angle sits BETWEEN the two equal sides — that is what makes it SAS. AAA is never a congruence criterion — equal angles give SIMILAR triangles, which may differ in size.

forms.title: Lines of symmetry and rotational order
forms.skill: For a regular n-gon both are n; irregular shapes break the pattern.

variants.statement: How many LINES of symmetry does a square have?
variants.explanation: A square has $4$ lines of symmetry. For a regular $n$-gon the count is exactly $n$ — the same as its rotational order, which is why the two are easy to conflate.

variants.statement: What is the ORDER of rotational symmetry of a square?
variants.explanation: Turning a square through $\frac{360°}{4}$ maps it onto itself, so the order is $4$ — the number of positions in one full turn.

variants.statement: What is the ORDER of rotational symmetry of a regular 20-gon?
variants.explanation: Turning a regular 20-gon through $\frac{360°}{20}$ maps it onto itself, so the order is $20$ — the number of positions in one full turn.

variants.statement: A point undergoes a reflection in the $x$-axis then a reflection in the $y$-axis. What single transformation has the same effect? (Check with $(3,\ 1) \mapsto (-3,\ -1)$.)

a rotation of $90°$ anticlockwise about the origin
a reflection in the line $y = x$

forms.title: Partitioning a segment in a ratio
forms.skill: Travel r/(r+s) of the way from the named endpoint — the end you start from matters.

variants.statement: Point $P$ divides the segment from $A(0,\ 0)$ to $B(8,\ 12)$ in the ratio $1:3$ (measured from $A$). Find $P$.
variants.explanation: Travel $\frac{1}{4}$ of the way from $A$ to $B$: $P = A + \frac{1}{4}(B - A) = (2,\ 3)$. Applying the ratio from the wrong end swaps the weights, and the midpoint is only right when the ratio is $1:1$.

variants.statement: Classify the quadrilateral with vertices $(0,\ 0)$, $(3,\ 0)$, $(3,\ 3)$ and $(0,\ 3)$, in that order.
options: a rectangle that is not a square
a parallelogram that is not a rectangle
a trapezium (exactly one pair of parallel sides)
variants.explanation: Compare opposite sides by SLOPE (parallel?) and by LENGTH (equal?), then check whether adjacent sides are perpendicular. Those three tests separate every option here — this figure is a square.

forms.title: Slope from two points
forms.skill: Rise over run — the y-difference goes on top.

variants.statement: Find the slope of the line through $(-5,\ -11)$ and $(-3,\ -17)$.
variants.explanation: Slope is rise over run: $\frac{-17 - (-11)}{-3 - (-5)} = \frac{-6}{2} = -3$. Putting the $x$-difference on top inverts the slope, which describes a completely different line.

forms.title: Reading a two-way frequency table
forms.skill: The denominator is the question: row total, column total, or grand total.

variants.statement: A survey gives this two-way table — Group 1: $30$ yes, $20$ no; Group 2: $10$ yes, $40$ no. What fraction of GROUP 1 answered yes?
variants.explanation: 'Of Group 1' restricts to that row, so the denominator is that row's total $30 + 20 = 50$: $\frac{30}{50} = \frac{3}{5}$. Dividing by the grand total $100$ would answer a different question.

variants.statement: A survey gives this two-way table — Group 1: $30$ yes, $20$ no; Group 2: $10$ yes, $40$ no. What fraction of EVERYONE surveyed is in Group 1 and answered yes?
variants.explanation: This is a JOINT proportion, so the denominator is the grand total $100$: $\frac{30}{100} = \frac{3}{10}$. The conditional version $\frac{3}{5}$ uses the row total instead.

variants.statement: A survey gives this two-way table — Group 1: $30$ yes, $20$ no; Group 2: $10$ yes, $40$ no. What fraction of everyone answered yes (either group)?
variants.explanation: Add the yes column across both groups: $30 + 10 = 40$, over the grand total $100$, giving $\frac{2}{5}$. This is the MARGINAL proportion.

forms.title: Interpreting a line of fit
forms.skill: Slope is change per unit; intercept is the prediction at zero; neither proves cause.

variants.statement: A line of best fit for study hours ($x$) against test score ($y$) is $y = 3x + 20$. What does the SLOPE mean?
options: each extra unit of study hours is associated with 3 points per hour
the predicted test score when study hours is zero
variants.explanation: The slope is the predicted CHANGE in $y$ per one-unit increase in $x$ — here $3$ points per hour. The intercept $20$ is the prediction at $x = 0$, and correlation strength is a separate quantity.

variants.statement: A line of best fit for study hours ($x$) against test score ($y$) is $y = 3x + 20$. What does the INTERCEPT mean?
options: each extra unit of study hours changes test score by 20
the predicted test score when study hours is zero
variants.explanation: Setting $x = 0$ gives $y = 20$, so the intercept is the predicted test score for zero study hours. Whether that is MEANINGFUL depends on whether $x = 0$ is inside the observed data.

variants.statement: Study hours and test score are strongly correlated. Someone concludes that changing study hours CAUSES the change in test score. What is the flaw?
options: the correlation is too weak to be real
the sample size must be too small
correlation does not establish causation — a confounding factor may drive both
the line of best fit was computed incorrectly
variants.explanation: Here students who study more may also sleep better and attend more classes, so a third factor plausibly moves both variables at once. A strong, correctly computed correlation on a large sample still cannot establish causation on its own — only a controlled experiment can.

forms.title: A missing value from the mean
forms.skill: Turn the mean into a total, then subtract what you already have.

variants.statement: Four numbers have mean $4$. Three of them are $5$, $5$ and $5$. Find the fourth.
variants.explanation: A mean of $4$ over four numbers means the TOTAL is $4 \times 4 = 16$. The three given add to $15$, so the fourth is $16 - 15 = 1$. Working with the total rather than the mean is what makes this one line.

forms.title: Adding a constant to every value
forms.skill: The centre moves with the shift; the spread does not move at all.

variants.statement: A data set has mean $12$ and range $6$. Every value is increased by $2$. What is the new mean?
variants.explanation: Adding the same amount to every value slides the whole data set along: the mean moves with it, $12 + 2 = 14$, while the RANGE stays $6$ because every gap between values is unchanged. Shift affects centre, not spread.

variants.statement: A data set has mean $12$ and range $6$. Every value is increased by $2$. What is the new range?
variants.explanation: Range is the largest value minus the smallest. Adding $2$ to both lifts them equally, so the difference is untouched: the range is still $6$. Only the centre moved.

forms.title: Summing an arithmetic sequence
forms.skill: Pair the ends: n/2 times (first + last).

variants.statement: An arithmetic sequence starts at $1$ and goes up by $2$ each time. Find the sum of its first $5$ terms.
variants.explanation: Pair the ends: the first term is $1$, the $5$th is $9$, and every pair sums to $10$. So the total is $\frac{5}{2}(1 + 9) = 25$. The LAST term $9$ is a different question from the total.

variants.statement: A room measures $3$ m by $4$ m. What is its area in SQUARE CENTIMETRES?

variants.statement: Solve $2x + c = 5x + d$ for $x$, where $c$ and $d$ are constants.
variants.explanation: The unknown is on BOTH sides, so it cannot be isolated by moving constants alone. Gather it: $2x - 5x = d - c$, which is $-3x = d - c$, so $x = \dfrac{d - c}{-3}$. Subtracting the two coefficients the other way flips the sign of the whole answer.

forms.skill: A one-off charge is a constant; a per-unit charge is a coefficient.

variants.statement: A taxi charges a flag-fall of $\$12$ dollars and $\$3$ dollars per kilometre. Write the cost as an expression in the number of kilometres, then find the cost for $8$ kilometres.
variants.explanation: The fee is charged ONCE, so it is a constant; the rate is charged per kilometre, so it is a coefficient. The expression is $3x + 12$, and at $8$ it gives $12 + 24 = 36$. Multiplying the fee by the count too is the standard error.

forms.title: What a parameter means
forms.skill: Each letter in a compound formula has a job — name it, do not guess.

variants.statement: A savings account is modelled by $A = 1000\left(1 + \dfrac{0.04}{2}\right)^{2 t}$, where $t$ is in years. What does the $2$ in TWO places of this formula represent?
options: The number of times interest is added per year — here, twice a year.
The number of years the money is invested.
The annual interest rate, as a percentage.
The number of dollars added each year.
variants.explanation: The annual rate $0.04$ is split into $2$ equal portions, and the exponent counts $2$ periods per year — so $2$ is the COMPOUNDING FREQUENCY, twice a year. The starting balance is $1000$ and the rate is $4\%$; neither is what the question asked about.

forms.title: Checking a candidate solution
forms.skill: Substitution always settles it, and it is never the wrong method.

variants.statement: Which value of $x$ satisfies $2x - 7 = 3x - 4$?
variants.explanation: Substituting $x = -3$ makes the left side $-13$ and the right side $-13$ — equal, so it is the solution. Checking a candidate by substitution is always available and never wrong.

forms.title: A budget, in words
forms.skill: A whole-object answer rounds DOWN, however close the next one is.

variants.statement: At a park a fairground ride costs $\$3$ and entry costs $\$8$. With $\$44$ to spend in total, what is the greatest number of rides affordable?
variants.explanation: The fee is paid once, leaving $44 - 8 = 36$ for the rides: $36 \div 3 = 12$, and you cannot buy a fraction of one, so the answer rounds DOWN to $12$. Rounding up would overspend.

forms.title: Is it a function?
forms.skill: One output per input. Repeating an OUTPUT is allowed.

variants.statement: A relation consists of the pairs $(1, 5)$, $(3, 5)$ and $(5, 6)$. Is it a function, and why?
options: Yes — each input appears with exactly one output.
No — two of the pairs share the same output.
No — an input is paired with two different outputs.
No — the outputs do not increase steadily.
variants.explanation: A function requires each INPUT to have exactly one output. The inputs $1$, $3$ and $5$ are all different, so the rule is satisfied. Two inputs sharing the OUTPUT $5$ is perfectly legal — that restriction runs the other way.

variants.statement: A relation consists of the pairs $(1, 5)$, $(1, 7)$ and $(3, 5)$. Is it a function, and why?
options: Yes — each input appears with exactly one output.
No — an input is paired with two different outputs.
No — two of the pairs share the same output.
Yes — every output is used at most twice.
variants.explanation: The input $1$ appears twice, once with output $5$ and once with output $7$. A function cannot give one input two answers, so this relation is not one. The repeated OUTPUT $5$ elsewhere would have been fine.

forms.title: Recursive against explicit
forms.skill: Reaching the nth term takes n - 1 steps, not n.

variants.statement: A sequence is defined by $a_1 = -5$ and $a_{n} = a_{n-1} + 2$. Which explicit formula gives the same sequence?
variants.explanation: The recursive rule adds $2$ each step, so the explicit form is first term plus $d$ times the number of STEPS taken — and reaching the $n$th term takes $n - 1$ steps, not $n$. Checking at $n = 1$ settles it: the correct formula gives $-5$, while the $2n$ version gives $-3$.

forms.title: First term past a threshold
forms.skill: 'Exceeds' is strict — landing exactly on the level does not count.

variants.statement: An arithmetic sequence starts at $5$ and increases by $3$ each term. Which term is the FIRST to exceed $55$?
variants.explanation: The $n$th term is $5 + 3(n-1)$. Term $17$ is $53$, which is still at most $55$; term $18$ is $56$, the first above it. 'Exceeds' means STRICTLY greater — landing exactly on $55$ would not count.

forms.title: A line from its two intercepts
forms.skill: The y-intercept is the constant; the x-intercept is not.

variants.statement: A line crosses the $x$-axis at $(-6, 0)$ and the $y$-axis at $(0, -9)$. What is its equation?
variants.explanation: Two points give the slope: $m = \dfrac{-9 - 0}{0 - (-6)} = -\frac{3}{2}$. The $y$-intercept is handed to you as $-9$, so $y = -\frac{3}{2}x - 9$. Using the $x$-intercept as the constant is the standard mix-up.

forms.title: When two plans cost the same
forms.skill: Set the two expressions equal; the gap closes at the rate difference.

variants.statement: Plan A costs $\$10$ up front plus $\$5$ per month. Plan B costs $\$22$ up front plus $\$3$ per month. After how many months do they cost the same?
variants.explanation: Set the two costs equal: $10 + 5n = 22 + 3n$. Collecting gives $2n = 12$, so $n = 6$. The cheaper start-up plan is behind by $\$12$ and catches up at $\$2$ per month.

forms.title: A tariff that changes rate
forms.skill: Only the amount ABOVE the break is charged at the higher rate.

variants.statement: An electricity tariff charges $6$ cents per kilowatt-hour for the first $20$ kilowatt-hours and $12$ cents per kilowatt-hour after that. What is the charge for $25$ kilowatt-hours?
variants.explanation: The first $20$ kilowatt-hours cost $20 \times 6 = 120$ cents. Only the $5$ kilowatt-hours ABOVE the break are charged at the higher rate: $5 \times 12 = 60$. Total $120 + 60 = 180$ cents. Charging the whole usage at the high rate is the standard error.

variants.statement: Line $\ell$ passes through $(1, 4)$ and is PARALLEL to $y = 2x - 4$. What is the $y$-coordinate of the point on $\ell$ where $x = 6$?
variants.explanation: Parallel means the SAME slope, $2$. Through $(1, 4)$: $4 = 2(1) + b$, so $b = 2$ and $\ell$ is $y = 2x + 2$. At $x = 6$: $2(6) + (2) = 14$. Using the original line's intercept $-4$ answers a different question.

forms.title: Where the model stops making sense
forms.skill: A model's domain is part of the model, not an afterthought.

variants.statement: A candle burns down according to $y = -2x + 24$, where $y$ is the height in centimetres and $t$ is the time in hours. For what values of $t$ does this model make sense?
variants.explanation: The model starts at $t = 0$ and the quantity runs out when $y = 0$: $-2x + 24 = 0$ gives $t = 12$. Beyond that the formula predicts a NEGATIVE height in centimetres, which is where the candle is used up and the model stops describing anything. The domain of a model is part of the model.

forms.title: Which pair solves BOTH
forms.skill: A solution must satisfy every equation, not just the convenient one.

variants.statement: Which ordered pair is the solution of the system $1x + 2y = -7$ and $x - y = -1$?
variants.explanation: A solution must satisfy BOTH equations. Substituting $(-3,\ -2)$: the first gives $1(-3) + 2(-2) = -7$ ✓ and the second gives $-3 - (-2) = -1$ ✓. Swapping the coordinates breaks at least one of them.

variants.statement: Which ordered pair is the solution of the system $1x + 2y = -1$ and $x - y = -4$?

forms.title: Two kinds, one total
forms.skill: A count equation and a value equation, solved together.

variants.statement: A shop sold $11$ tickets in total, some adult and some child, taking $74$ dollars altogether. A adult one is worth $9$ and a child one $4$. How many adult ones were sold?
variants.explanation: Let $x$ be the number of adult ones. Then $11 - x$ are child, and $9x + 4(11 - x) = 74$. Expanding gives $5x + 44 = 74$, so $5x = 30$ and $x = 6$. The other count, $5$, answers the other half of the question.

variants.explanation: Neither variable cancels as written, so scale first: multiplying the equations by $5$ and $2$ makes the $x$ terms match, and subtracting leaves one equation in $y$ alone. It solves to $y = 1$ (and then $x = -2$). Substituting both back into BOTH equations is the check.

forms.title: When the question wants x + y
forms.skill: Read what is asked before choosing a method — sometimes it is already there.

variants.statement: In the system $2x + 3y = -8$ and $x + y + 3 = 0$, what is the value of $x + y$?
variants.explanation: The second equation already contains $x + y$: $x + y = 0 - 3 = -3$. No solving for $x$ and $y$ separately is needed — and doing it would take three times as long for the same answer. Read the question before choosing a method.

forms.title: A point in BOTH regions
forms.skill: Test every candidate in every inequality; passing one is not enough.

variants.statement: Which point satisfies BOTH $y < x + 1$ and $x + y < 5$?
variants.explanation: Test each candidate in BOTH inequalities — passing one is not enough. $(1,\ 1)$ gives $1 < 2$ ✓ and $2 < 5$ ✓. $(1,\ 4)$ sits ABOVE the first line, so it fails there whatever the second says.

forms.title: Percentage to multiplier
forms.skill: Add to 1 for growth, subtract from 1 for decay — never use the bare percent.

variants.statement: A quantity INCREASES by $2\%$ each year. What is the growth factor?
variants.explanation: Keeping all of it and adding $2\%$ means multiplying by $1 + \frac{1}{50} = \frac{51}{50}$. The bare $\frac{1}{50}$ is the INCREASE alone, not the multiplier — using it would shrink the quantity to a fraction of itself.

variants.statement: A quantity DECREASES by $2\%$ each year. What is the decay factor?
variants.explanation: Losing $2\%$ leaves $98\%$, so the multiplier is $1 - \frac{1}{50} = \frac{49}{50}$. A decay factor is always between $0$ and $1$; a negative multiplier would flip the sign of the quantity every year.

forms.title: Writing the exponential model
forms.skill: Starting amount out front, multiplier as the base, time as the exponent.

variants.statement: A colony of bacteria starts at $200$ bacteria and grows by $5\%$ every hour. Which formula models it after $t$ hours?
variants.explanation: The starting amount is the coefficient, $200$. A grow of $5\%$ per hour multiplies by $\frac{21}{20}$ each time, so that is the base and $t$ is the exponent. A percentage change compounds — it is never added term by term, which is what the linear option does.

forms.title: First whole period past a level
forms.skill: Whole periods mean the answer rounds UP.

variants.statement: A population is modelled by $P = 3 \cdot 2^{t}$, with $t$ in years. After how many WHOLE years does the population first exceed $60$?
variants.explanation: At $t = 4$ the model gives $48$, still at most $60$; at $t = 5$ it gives $96$, which is past it. So the answer is $5$ years. Because $t$ counts whole years, the answer must round UP — the model crosses the level part-way through the year.

forms.title: Recovering a and b
forms.skill: t = 0 hands you a; the other point needs a root, not a division.

variants.statement: An exponential model $y = a \cdot b^{t}$ passes through $(0, 2)$ and $(2, 8)$. What are $a$ and $b$?
variants.explanation: At $t = 0$ every power is $1$, so $a = 2$ is read straight off. Then $2 \cdot b^{2} = 8$ gives $b^{2} = 4$, and taking the $2$th root leaves $b = 2$. Skipping the root gives $4$, the growth over all $2$ periods rather than per period.

forms.title: Same growth, different period

variants.statement: A quantity multiplies by $8$ every year. By what factor does it multiply in each four-month period, of which there are $3$ in a year?
variants.explanation: The $3$ periods must MULTIPLY to the annual factor, not add to it: $x^{3} = 8$, so $x = 2$ (check: $2^{3} = 8$). Dividing the annual factor by $3$ treats compound growth as if it were linear, which is the whole distinction this unit is about.

forms.title: Reflecting in an axis
forms.skill: The axis you reflect in is the coordinate that SURVIVES.

variants.statement: The point $(-6,\ -5)$ is reflected in the $x$-axis. What are the coordinates of the image?
variants.explanation: Reflecting in the $x$-axis flips the point over that axis, so the horizontal position is untouched and the vertical one changes sign: $(x,\ y) \to (x,\ -y)$, giving $(-6,\ 5)$. Negating $x$ instead reflects in the $y$-axis.

variants.statement: The point $(-6,\ -5)$ is reflected in the $y$-axis. What are the coordinates of the image?
variants.explanation: Reflecting in the $y$-axis keeps the height and flips the side: $(x,\ y) \to (-x,\ y)$, giving $(6,\ -5)$. The axis you reflect in is the one whose coordinate SURVIVES.

forms.title: Rotating about the origin
forms.skill: A quarter turn swaps the coordinates and negates one of them.

variants.statement: The point $(-5,\ -6)$ is rotated $90°$ ANTICLOCKWISE about the origin. What are the coordinates of the image?
variants.explanation: A quarter turn anticlockwise sends $(x,\ y)$ to $(-y,\ x)$, so $(-5,\ -6)$ lands on $(6,\ -5)$. The CLOCKWISE quarter turn is the other one, $(y,\ -x)$ — the two differ by a half turn.

variants.statement: The point $(-5,\ -6)$ is rotated $180°$ about the origin. What are the coordinates of the image?
variants.explanation: A half turn sends every point to the opposite side of the origin: $(x,\ y) \to (-x,\ -y)$, giving $(5,\ 6)$. Both coordinates change sign, which is what makes a half turn the same clockwise or anticlockwise.

variants.statement: Triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $PQR$, and $AB = 5$. Which side of the second triangle must also measure $5$?
variants.explanation: A congruence statement is an ORDER: $A \to P$, $B \to Q$, $C \to R$. So $AB$ corresponds to $PQ$, and corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal. Reading the letters out of order is what produces the wrong side.

forms.title: Angles on a transversal
forms.skill: Alternate means equal; co-interior means supplementary.

variants.statement: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One of the co-interior angles measures $35°$. What is the other co-interior angle?
variants.explanation: Co-interior angles lie between the parallel lines on the SAME side of the transversal, and they are supplementary: $180° - 35° = 145°$. Equal is what ALTERNATE angles are — the opposite sides of the transversal.

variants.statement: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. An alternate interior angle pair includes an angle of $35°$. What is the angle co-interior to that same angle?
variants.explanation: The alternate angle equals $35°$; the CO-INTERIOR angle sits beside it on a straight line, so it is $180° - 35° = 145°$. Alternate means equal, co-interior means supplementary — which side of the transversal you are on decides which.

forms.title: Angle relationships as equations
forms.skill: Corresponding angles are EQUAL — that is what makes an equation.

variants.statement: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. A pair of CORRESPONDING angles measure $2x + 16$ and $4x + 4$ degrees. Find $x$.
variants.explanation: Corresponding angles between parallel lines are EQUAL, so $2x + 16 = 4x + 4$. Collecting gives $2x = 12$, hence $x = 6$; both expressions then give $28°$, which is the check. Treating the pair as supplementary — making them sum to $180°$ — is the commonest wrong move, and it is what CO-INTERIOR angles do, not corresponding ones.

variants.statement: Two angles of a triangle measure $28°$ and $35°$. What is the EXTERIOR angle at the third vertex?
variants.explanation: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two REMOTE interior angles: $28 + 35 = 63°$. The third INTERIOR angle is $180 - 28 - 35 = 117°$, and indeed $63 + 117 = 180$ — the two form a linear pair.

forms.title: Perimeter from coordinates
forms.skill: Three distances, added — and the hypotenuse is the one people drop.

variants.statement: A triangle has vertices $(0,\ 0)$, $(3,\ 0)$ and $(0,\ 4)$. What is its perimeter?
variants.explanation: Two sides are along the axes, of lengths $3$ and $4$. The third joins $(3,\ 0)$ to $(0,\ 4)$: $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$. The perimeter is $3 + 4 + 5 = 12$. Note the area, $\frac{1}{2}(3)(4) = 6$, is a different quantity.

forms.title: Area from three vertices
forms.skill: The bracket gives TWICE the area — the half is not optional.

variants.statement: A triangle has vertices $(0,\ 0)$, $(4,\ 0)$ and $(3,\ 6)$. What is its area?
variants.explanation: Using the coordinate area formula, $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}\left|x_A(y_B - y_C) + x_B(y_C - y_A) + x_C(y_A - y_B)\right|$, the bracket comes to $24$ and half of it is $12$. Forgetting the half is the standard error — that quantity is twice the area, which is the area of the surrounding parallelogram.

forms.title: What proves a parallelogram
forms.skill: Equal slopes on both pairs of opposite sides, and nothing more.

variants.statement: A quadrilateral has vertices $(0,\ 0)$, $(3,\ 0)$, $(8,\ 5)$ and $(5,\ 5)$, in order. Which single coordinate check PROVES it is a parallelogram?
options: Both pairs of opposite sides have equal slopes.
All four sides have the same length.
The four vertices are all in different quadrants.
variants.explanation: A parallelogram is DEFINED by both pairs of opposite sides being parallel, and parallel means equal slope — so that is the check that proves it and nothing more is needed. Equal side lengths would prove a RHOMBUS and equal diagonals a RECTANGLE; both are stronger claims than the question asks for, and neither follows from being a parallelogram.

variants.statement: $P$ is $(1,\ 2)$ and $Q$ is $(3,\ 6)$. For angle $PQR$ to be a RIGHT angle, which point could $R$ be?
variants.explanation: $PQ$ has slope $\dfrac{6 - (2)}{3 - (1)} = 2$. A right angle at $Q$ needs $QR$ perpendicular, so its slope must be the negative reciprocal $-\frac{1}{2}$. From $Q$, moving $4$ right and $2$ down reaches $(7,\ 4)$, and $2 \times -\frac{1}{2} = -1$ confirms it.

forms.title: Mode and median
forms.skill: Sort before reading a median; the mode needs no sorting at all.

variants.statement: A data set is $5,\ 3,\ 2,\ 7,\ 3$. What is the MODE?
variants.explanation: The mode is the value that appears most often. Only $3$ occurs twice; every other value occurs once. The median — the middle of the SORTED list — is also $3$ here, but that is a coincidence of this data set, not a rule.

variants.statement: A data set is $5,\ 3,\ 2,\ 7,\ 3$. What is the MEDIAN?
variants.explanation: Sort first: $2,\ 3,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7$. With five values the median is the third, $3$. Taking the middle of the list AS PRINTED gives $2$ instead.

forms.title: Same centre, different spread

forms.title: Percentages inside a table
forms.skill: The words 'of the ...' name the denominator.

variants.statement: In a survey, $9$ students who cycle and $9$ students who walk said they enjoy the journey, while $6$ cyclists and $14$ walkers did not. What PERCENTAGE of the cyclists enjoy the journey?
variants.explanation: 'Of the cyclists' fixes the denominator: there are $9 + 6 = 15$ cyclists in total, and $9$ of them enjoy it, so $\dfrac{9}{15} = 60\%$. Dividing by everyone surveyed, or by all the enjoyers, answers a different question.

forms.title: Residuals and their sign
forms.skill: Observed minus predicted — reversing it reverses the story.

variants.statement: A line of best fit is $y = 2x + 1$. At $x = 2$ the observed value is $-1$. What is the residual, and does the model over- or under-predict?
variants.explanation: Residual means observed MINUS predicted: the model predicts $2(2) + 1 = 5$, so the residual is $-1 - 5 = -6$. A negative residual means the point sits below the line, so the model over-predicts there. Reversing the subtraction reverses the story.

forms.title: What an association licenses
forms.skill: Correlation is real evidence of association and no evidence of cause.

variants.statement: A study finds a correlation of $0.62$ between hours of sleep and test scores. Which conclusion is supported?
options: The two vary together; the study alone cannot show that one causes the other.
Hours of sleep causes test scores, because the correlation is strong.
Introducing a tutoring programme will therefore change test scores.
There is no relationship, because correlation is never meaningful.
variants.explanation: A correlation of $0.62$ is real and worth reporting — the two quantities do move together. But an OBSERVATIONAL study cannot rule out a lurking variable driving both, or the causation running the other way. Only a randomised experiment licenses a causal claim, and only for the population it sampled.

forms.title: Adding one extreme value
forms.skill: The mean feels a value's SIZE; the median only feels its position.

variants.statement: The values $3,\ 5,\ 7,\ 9,\ 11$ have mean $7$ and median $7$. The value $43$ is now added to the set. Which statement is true?
options: The mean rises by much more than the median does.
The median rises by much more than the mean does.
The mean and the median rise by the same amount.
Neither the mean nor the median changes.
variants.explanation: The new value is far above the rest. The mean uses every value's SIZE, so it climbs from $7$ to $13$. The median only cares about POSITION, and with six values it becomes the average of the middle two: $8$ — a small move. That difference in sensitivity is why the median is preferred for skewed data.
